questions.question: Which alphabet positions are 'prime' among 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 (letters B, C, E, G, K, M)?
options: All of them, since 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 are all prime numbers
Only 2 and 3
None of them
Only the even ones
questions.rationale: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13 are all prime numbers, making B, C, E, G, K, and M the letters at prime alphabet positions in that range.

questions.question: What are 'composite alphabet positions'?
options: Positions that are prime
Only even positions
Positions that are not prime and not 1 (i.e., have factors other than 1 and themselves)
Only positions above 20
questions.rationale: Composite positions are those with factors other than 1 and themselves — the counterpart to prime positions, excluding position 1 (which is neither prime nor composite).

questions.question: What does 'odd and even alphabet positions' coding distinguish?
options: Vowels from consonants
Letters at odd-numbered positions (A, C, E...) from letters at even-numbered positions (B, D, F...), often treating each group differently
Uppercase from lowercase letters
The first half of the alphabet from the second half
questions.rationale: This coding groups letters by whether their alphabet position number is odd or even, and often applies a different rule to each group.

questions.question: What is 'binary-style letter coding'?
options: Coding using only two letters
Representing each letter's position as a binary (base-2) number instead of a decimal one
A rule with no numeric component
Coding that only works for the letters A and B
questions.rationale: Binary-style coding expresses a letter's numeric value (like its alphabet position) in base-2 (binary) notation rather than ordinary base-10.

questions.question: What does 'reverse position coding' use as a letter's value?
options: Its position counted from the end of the alphabet (i.e., its reverse-alphabet position) rather than from the start
Its normal alphabet position
A random assigned value
The number of times it appears in the word
questions.rationale: Reverse position coding uses a letter's reverse-alphabet position (counted from Z backward) as its value, rather than its normal position counted from A.

questions.question: What does 'sum of reverse positions' compute?
options: The sum of normal alphabet positions
Only the first letter's reverse position
The total of all the letters' reverse-alphabet position values in a word
The product of reverse positions
questions.rationale: This computes the sum of each letter's reverse-alphabet position (27 minus its normal position) across the whole word.

questions.question: What is 'mirror coding'?
options: Reversing the order of the letters
Replacing each letter with its reverse-alphabet partner (the letter it's mirrored with around the center of the alphabet)
Doubling every letter's position
A rule with no relationship to the reverse alphabet
questions.rationale: Mirror coding replaces each letter with its reverse-alphabet counterpart — the letter it mirrors with around the alphabet's center point.

questions.question: What does 'mirror + shift coding' combine?
options: Two separate shifts with no mirroring
A rule identical to plain mirror coding
Only word reversal, no letter transformation
First mirroring each letter to its reverse-alphabet partner, then applying an additional shift to that result
questions.rationale: This combines two steps: first mirror each letter to its reverse-alphabet partner, and then apply a further shift to that mirrored result.

questions.question: What is 'word reversal coding'?
options: Reversing the order of the letters in the word, without changing the letters themselves
Reversing each individual letter's shape
Replacing letters with their mirror partners
Shifting each letter by the word's length
questions.rationale: Word reversal coding simply reverses the order in which the letters appear, leaving the letters themselves unchanged.

questions.question: Under mirror coding, what does the letter D (position 4) map to?
options: V
W
X
Y
questions.rationale: D is position 4; its reverse-alphabet partner is at position 27-4=23, which is W.
